summaries.example: Imagine building a small house from bricks. The bricks are the matter: the stuff used to make it. The house-plan and the way the bricks are organized are like the form: what makes the bricks into one house rather than just a pile. If the bricks are later used to make a wall, the same matter has taken part in a new object.
summaries.summary: Aristotle uses matter and form to explain physical things and the changes they undergo. Matter is the stuff that makes something up, while form is what makes that stuff organized as a particular kind of thing. For example, bricks can become a house when arranged and used in the right way. In a change where a new object comes into existence, some underlying matter must remain; otherwise something would come from nothing. Aristotle thinks this is impossible. He also distinguishes changes that merely alter an existing thing from changes in which a thing begins or ends. His idea becomes more complicated for living things. A human body is not just a shape: it must be able to perform the activities of a living human. Aristotle also describes matter in layers, from an object’s nearest materials down to more basic ingredients. Scholars debate whether there is an ultimate “prime matter” beneath everything, whether matter explains why individuals are different, and whether a natural thing’s form includes the kind of matter it needs.
key_ideas: Aristotle says physical things are made from matter and form together.
Matter helps explain what persists when something changes; form helps explain what the thing is.
Form is not always a shape. A living thing’s form includes its abilities and way of functioning.
Matter can be discussed at different levels: a house may be made of bricks, bricks of clay, and so on.
Philosophers disagree about whether Aristotle believed in a final, completely changeable matter called prime matter.
They also debate whether matter, form, or neither explains why two similar things are two different individuals.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea gives one way to ask what objects are, how they stay connected through change, and what makes living things more than arrangements of parts. It also shows why simple questions can become difficult: the same material may take different forms, but a living body seems closely tied to its life-activities. Aristotle’s proposal influenced later philosophy and continues to inspire discussion.

important_terms.definition: The material or stuff that something is made from. Aristotle also uses matter for what remains through some kinds of change.
What makes something the kind of thing it is, including its organization, nature, or job—not merely its outside shape.
Aristotle’s view that ordinary physical things involve both matter and form.
A change in which a thing gains or loses a feature while remaining the same thing, such as becoming blue.
A change in which a thing begins or stops existing as a particular kind of thing.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a pile of blocks become one toy house?
Can something have the same material but become a different object?
Is a statue shaped like a person a person? Why or why not?
What might be good or difficult about believing that everything has both matter and form?

summaries.example: Consider an acorn becoming an oak. The oak’s form is not merely its visible outline. It includes the organization and capacities that make it an oak and enable its characteristic activities. Its matter exists at several levels: the living body is relatively near to the form, while tissues and more basic elements are farther down the material hierarchy. This helps explain why the acorn-to-oak process is not creation from nothing, even though the mature organism did not previously exist.
summaries.summary: Aristotle introduces matter and form in the Physics as resources for explaining change without allowing things to arise from nothing. Accidental change involves a substance that persists while gaining or losing a property; substantial change involves a substance’s coming to be or passing away, so matter must underlie the transition. Form is not simply geometrical shape. It is the essence or defining organization of a thing, closely connected with its characteristic activities and, in Aristotle’s account of causes, often with its function. The analysis becomes difficult for organisms, since an organism’s proximate matter appears to be essentially alive, while the theory also requires some material basis that can exist before or after the organism. Aristotle’s layered account of matter—proximate, more remote, and ultimately elemental—offers one response. A further question is whether elemental change requires prime matter, a wholly indeterminate substrate. The entry presents arguments for and against attributing this doctrine to Aristotle. It also distinguishes unity from individuation: form can explain how parts constitute one object, but it is less clear what explains why one member of a species is numerically distinct from another. Finally, the entry examines whether natural forms themselves include material specifications. Several interpretations are possible, and stronger versions risk an infinite regress of forms.
key_ideas: Aristotle’s hylomorphic framework analyzes ordinary physical substances as compounds of matter and form, especially to explain substantial generation and destruction.

In any change, Aristotle distinguishes an underlying subject, a lack or contrary starting condition, and an acquired form. For substantial change, matter plays the underlying role because the substance itself does not persist as the same substance.

Form is identified with essence and is tied to function. Thus the form of an organism cannot be reduced to its shape, and a dead body may count as a body only in a derivative sense if it cannot perform bodily functions.

Matter is relative and layered: what is matter at one level can be a form-matter compound at another. This helps address how an organism can have living proximate matter while more remote materials persist independently.

The traditional interpretation attributes prime matter to Aristotle as pure potentiality, but other interpreters argue that the texts leave this open or that the doctrine creates serious explanatory problems.

The individuation debate separates unity from numerical distinctness. Form may unify parts into one object, while matter, particular forms, or even no further principle may be proposed to explain why similar individuals are distinct.
summaries.why_it_matters: Hylomorphism is not merely a historical vocabulary for materials and shapes. It is a theory about composition, identity through change, essence, function, and explanation. Its problems reveal tensions that remain important in metaphysics: whether an underlying substrate must be posited, whether objects are more than their current parts, and whether a thing’s nature can be specified independently of its material realization. The framework has also been applied in Aristotle’s discussions of soul and body and political organization, although this entry concentrates on its physical and metaphysical foundations.

important_terms.definition: The matter nearest to a thing in the explanatory hierarchy; for an organism, this may be its organized living body.
A proposed ultimate substrate with no essential properties of its own, capable of receiving any form. Scholars dispute whether Aristotle is committed to it.
A proposed answer to what makes one individual numerically distinct from another, rather than merely making it a unified whole.
The feature or structure that accounts for something being one organized object rather than a mere collection of parts.
A view that a natural form or essence includes, or necessarily refers to, suitable material conditions.
The nature or definition of a thing—what it is to be that kind of thing.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining change require something that literally persists, or could an initial state merely lead to a later one?
If prime matter has no essential properties, how can it be described without contradiction?
Are “what makes an object one” and “what makes it different from another object” genuinely separate questions?
If two people could successively contain the same matter, would matter alone explain their numerical distinctness?
Should a natural form include material conditions, or can matter and form retain sharply separate explanatory roles?

summaries.example: Suppose a school turns an old wooden table into several shelves. The wood is matter because it continues through the change, while the arrangement and purpose that make the result shelves are related to form. The same wood can belong first to a table and later to shelves. But if we ask what makes two wooden shelves two different objects, the answer is less obvious: their shapes, their pieces of wood, their histories, or something else? This is the kind of puzzle Aristotle’s theory raises.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s form-and-matter theory begins with a problem about change. If a new substance comes to be, it cannot appear from nothing, so something must underlie the change. In an artifact, this might be wood or bricks. In a living thing, the issue is harder because the body seems to be organized for life, and Aristotle treats the form of a living thing as connected with its activities rather than with outward shape alone. Matter can be understood in levels: the material nearest to an object may itself be made from more basic material. This leads to the question of prime matter. On the traditional reading, prime matter is pure potentiality beneath the elements. Other scholars question whether Aristotle really endorses this view, noting that it is difficult to describe something that has no essential properties. The entry also examines individuation. Form may explain how many parts make one unified object, while matter has traditionally been said to explain why two members of one species are numerically different. Yet puzzles arise if the same matter could later make up different individuals. A final dispute asks whether natural forms are pure or whether they include necessary references to matter. The entry presents these interpretations without treating the disagreements as settled.
key_ideas: Matter and form work together to explain what physical things are and how they change.
For substantial change, Aristotle needs some underlying matter, because he rejects the idea that something can come from absolutely nothing.
Form means more than shape. For living things, it includes the abilities and organization needed for their characteristic activities.
Matter is relative: bricks can be matter for a house, while clay can be matter for bricks, and still more basic materials can underlie clay.
Some interpreters think elemental change requires prime matter; others argue that Aristotle does not clearly commit to it or that the idea is difficult to make coherent.
The debate about individuation may concern two different questions: what unifies parts into one object and what makes one object numerically distinct from another.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory matters because it connects several questions that students often meet separately: what an object is made of, what makes it the kind of object it is, how it changes, and what makes it one individual. It also helps explain why defining a living thing is not the same as describing its appearance. Studying the disagreements shows how philosophers test a theory by comparing its concepts, examples, textual evidence, and consequences.

important_terms.definition: The stuff that underlies or makes up an object, such as wood, bricks, flesh, or more basic elements.
The organization, nature, or defining way of functioning that makes matter a particular kind of thing.
Aristotle’s theory that physical objects are compounds of matter and form.
A change in an existing substance’s properties while the substance remains, such as becoming blue or learning a skill.
A change in which a substance comes into existence or ceases to exist as that substance.
A proposed basis for why one individual is numerically different from another individual of the same kind.
A proposed ultimate matter with no built-in features of its own; scholars disagree about whether Aristotle accepts it.

questions_to_think_about: When a table becomes shelves, what remains the same?
Why might a human body be more than a particular shape?
Would an ultimate matter with no properties help explain change, or make explanation harder?
Can form explain why something is one whole without explaining why it is different from another similar thing?
Should the definition of an animal mention the material it must have?
